questions.question: Roughly how much GPU memory do the weights of a 7-billion-parameter model need in FP16, before any KV cache or activations?
options: About 14 GB
About 7 MB
About 28 GB
About 3.5 GB
questions.explanation: FP16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, so 7B × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB. INT8 would be about 7 GB, INT4 about 3.5 GB, and FP32 about 28 GB. The KV cache and runtime overhead come on top.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: A 70B-parameter model must fit on a single 80 GB GPU for inference. Which choice makes the weights fit with the most room for the KV cache?
options: Keep FP16 weights (about 140 GB)
Quantize the weights to 4-bit (about 35 GB)
Convert to FP32 for accuracy (about 280 GB)
Increase the batch size
questions.explanation: At 2 bytes per parameter a 70B model needs about 140 GB in FP16, which doesn't fit. INT4/FP4 weight quantization brings it to about 35 GB, leaving memory for the KV cache. Otherwise, tensor parallelism over several GPUs is needed.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: GPU memory runs out when many users send long prompts to an LLM server, even though the weights fit comfortably. Which two factors directly increase KV cache memory? (Select two.)
options: Longer sequence lengths (prompt plus output tokens)
More concurrent requests in the batch
A shorter system prompt shared by all of the requests
Using top-p (nucleus) sampling instead of top-k sampling
A lower sampling temperature for every request in the batch
questions.explanation: KV cache size scales with batch_size × sequence_length × 2 × num_layers × hidden_size × bytes per value. More concurrent requests and longer contexts both grow it linearly. Sampling settings don't affect it, and a shorter prompt reduces it.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: What does the KV cache store during autoregressive generation?
options: Keys and values of previous tokens, so they aren't recomputed
Final answers of previous users, so repeated questions are fast
The tokenizer vocabulary, so tokens are decoded more quickly
The gradients from the last training step, for continual learning
questions.explanation: Each new token attends to all previous tokens. Caching their keys and values avoids recomputing them at every decoding step, at the cost of GPU memory that grows with sequence length and batch size.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: LLM inference has a prefill phase and a decode phase. Which statement is correct?
options: Prefill is memory-bound, token by token; decode is compute-bound and parallel
Prefill is compute-bound and parallel; decode is memory-bound, token by token
Both phases generate one token at a time and are compute-bound
Decode runs first to plan the answer, then prefill processes the prompt
questions.explanation: Prefill computes keys and values for all input tokens at once, which saturates compute. Decode produces one token per step and must read the weights and KV cache each time, so it is limited by memory bandwidth. That is why batching helps decode throughput.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: What do multi-query attention (MQA) and grouped-query attention (GQA) reduce compared with standard multi-head attention?
options: The number of layers, by sharing weights across adjacent layers
The vocabulary size, by sharing token embeddings across heads
The KV cache size, by sharing key/value heads across query heads
The training data needed, by sharing examples across query heads
questions.explanation: MQA shares a single key/value head across all query heads. GQA shares K/V within groups of query heads, which is a middle ground. Both shrink the KV cache and memory traffic. MQA may cost some accuracy, and GQA balances the two (Llama 2 70B uses GQA).

source.title: Ainslie et al., GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models

questions.question: Which two statements about FlashAttention are correct? (Select two.)
options: It moves the attention computation onto the CPU
It works in tiles held in fast on-chip memory, cutting HBM reads and writes
It computes exact attention, not an approximation
It removes the softmax from attention to save time
It drops most tokens to make the attention matrix sparse
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is an IO-aware, exact attention algorithm. Tiling and recomputation avoid materializing the full n×n matrix in GPU HBM, which saves memory and time without changing the results.

source.title: Dao et al., FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention

questions.question: Which two statements about speculative decoding are correct? (Select two.)
options: It lowers the target model's precision to 1 bit during generation
It helps most at low batch sizes, where decoding is memory-bound
It answers from a cache of earlier users' outputs when prompts are similar
A cheap draft proposes tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass
It skips the tokenizer for the most common words to save time per step
questions.explanation: A draft model or extra heads guess several tokens, and the target model checks them in parallel, accepting the longest correct prefix. With proper acceptance sampling the output distribution matches the target model's. It mainly speeds up low-batch, latency-sensitive decoding.

source.title: TensorRT-LLM, Speculative Decoding

questions.question: Which two benefits are the main reasons to quantize an LLM from FP16 to INT8 or FP8 for inference? (Select two.)
options: No GPU needed at all once the model has been quantized
A longer context window, because tokens use fewer bits
Higher throughput from faster low-precision Tensor Core math
Guaranteed higher accuracy on every benchmark after quantization
Lower memory use for the weights and KV cache
questions.explanation: Lower-precision values take fewer bytes, so the model needs less memory and bandwidth, and reduced-precision Tensor Core math is faster. Accuracy can drop slightly, so it must be measured. Quantization doesn't extend the context window.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: What is the difference between post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT)?
options: PTQ quantizes activations only; QAT quantizes the tokenizer vocabulary
PTQ applies only to CPU inference; QAT applies only to GPU inference
PTQ quantizes a trained model; QAT simulates quantization while training
PTQ quantizes during training; QAT quantizes after the model is deployed
questions.explanation: PTQ is fast and needs no retraining, using a small calibration set to pick scales. QAT inserts fake-quantization operations during training or fine-tuning, so it usually recovers more accuracy at low bit widths but costs training time.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Achieving FP32 Accuracy for INT8 Inference Using QAT

questions.question: Why does INT8 post-training quantization of activations need a calibration dataset?
options: To estimate activation ranges and choose good scaling factors
To measure test accuracy after quantization has finished
To retrain the model's weights from scratch in INT8 precision
To prune the layers that are least useful for the target task
questions.explanation: Mapping FP values to 256 integer levels requires a scale. Calibration runs representative inputs through the model to estimate activation ranges, so the chosen scales cover real data without clipping too much or wasting resolution.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Achieving FP32 Accuracy for INT8 Inference Using QAT

questions.question: AWQ and GPTQ are examples of:
options: Weight-only quantization methods for LLMs, e.g. 4-bit weights
Approximate nearest-neighbour index types for vector databases
Distributed training strategies for very large models
Prompt engineering techniques for structured JSON output
questions.explanation: GPTQ and AWQ (activation-aware weight quantization) compress LLM weights to about 3-4 bits with little accuracy loss and keep activations in higher precision. TensorRT-LLM supports them, for example in W4A16 AWQ/GPTQ recipes.

source.title: TensorRT-LLM, Quantization

questions.question: Knowledge distillation reduces inference cost by:
options: Caching the teacher's answers and returning them to users
Training a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher
Removing the attention heads that contribute least to the output
Splitting the large model across more GPUs to share the load
questions.explanation: In distillation a compact student learns from the teacher's outputs (soft probabilities), which transfers much of its ability. The student is cheaper and faster to serve.

source.title: Hinton et al., Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network

questions.question: NVIDIA Ampere and later Tensor Cores accelerate a specific structured sparsity pattern. Which one?
options: Layer sparsity: every second Transformer layer is removed
Embedding sparsity: only the embedding table holds zeros
Unstructured sparsity: any random 90% of values are zero
2:4 sparsity: two out of every four values are zero
questions.explanation: Structured 2:4 sparsity, with two non-zeros in every group of four, is supported in hardware by Sparse Tensor Cores and can roughly double math throughput for those layers. Unstructured random sparsity is hard to accelerate.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: A model is too large for one GPU, so its weight matrices are split across GPUs and each GPU computes part of every layer. What is this called?
options: Data parallelism
Tensor parallelism
Pipeline parallelism
Gradient accumulation
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism shards individual layers 'horizontally' (e.g. splitting matrix multiplications), as in Megatron-LM. It needs very fast interconnect such as NVLink. Pipeline parallelism instead assigns whole layers to different GPUs.

source.title: Shoeybi et al., Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism

questions.question: In pipeline parallelism, consecutive groups of layers run on different GPUs. What inefficiency must be managed, typically with micro-batches?
options: Pipeline bubbles: GPUs idle while waiting for other stages
Token drift: later stages see differently tokenized inputs
KV overflow: the first stage stores the whole KV cache
Gradient decay: gradients are always zero on later stages
questions.explanation: Without overlapping, later stages wait for earlier ones (and vice versa in the backward pass), which leaves GPUs idle. Splitting each batch into micro-batches keeps more stages busy at once, as in GPipe.

source.title: Huang et al., GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism

questions.question: In data-parallel training on 8 GPUs, which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Only GPU 0 updates its weights; the other GPUs only run inference
Each GPU stores a different slice of every weight matrix in the model
Mini-batches are sent back to the CPU, which performs the weight update
Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and processes different data
Gradients are averaged across GPUs with an all-reduce every step
questions.explanation: In data parallelism every GPU has a full replica and a different shard of the batch. An all-reduce (e.g. via NCCL) averages the gradients so all replicas apply the same update. Splitting weight matrices across GPUs is tensor parallelism.

source.title: NVIDIA NCCL User Guide, Overview

questions.question: Roughly how much GPU memory does full fine-tuning of a 7B model with Adam in mixed precision need for weights, gradients and optimizer states (excluding activations)?
options: About 7 GB (1 byte per parameter)
About 14 GB (2 bytes per parameter)
About 112 GB (about 16 bytes per parameter)
About 1 TB (about 150 bytes per parameter)
questions.explanation: Mixed-precision Adam typically needs 2 bytes (FP16 weights) + 2 (gradients) + 12 (FP32 master weights, momentum and variance) ≈ 16 bytes per parameter, so 7B × 16 ≈ 112 GB. This is why PEFT methods such as LoRA and sharding (ZeRO/FSDP) are popular.

source.title: Rajbhandari et al., ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models

questions.question: What problem does loss scaling solve in FP16 mixed-precision training?
options: Large FP16 losses overflow the logs; scaling hides them
FP16 needs no optimizer; scaling replaces Adam's updates
Small FP16 gradients underflow to zero; scaling keeps them
FP16 weights drift apart across GPUs; scaling syncs them
questions.explanation: FP16 has a narrow exponent range, so tiny gradients can underflow. Multiplying the loss by a scale factor before backpropagation, and unscaling before the weight update, preserves them. BF16 has FP32's exponent range and usually doesn't need it.

source.title: NVIDIA, Train With Mixed Precision (User Guide)

questions.question: A fine-tuning job runs out of GPU memory. Which two techniques reduce memory without changing the model architecture? (Select two.)
options: Gradient accumulation over smaller micro-batches
Increasing the per-step batch size to use the GPU fully
Disabling the learning-rate scheduler and warmup
Switching from BF16 to FP32 for more stable gradients
Gradient checkpointing (recompute activations)
questions.explanation: Checkpointing stores fewer activations and recomputes them, trading compute for memory. Gradient accumulation uses small micro-batches and sums gradients over several steps to get the same effective batch. Bigger batches and FP32 increase memory.

source.title: Chen et al., Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost

questions.question: Users of a chat app complain that it 'feels slow to start answering', although total generation time is fine. Which metric should the team look at first?
options: Time to first token (TTFT)
Total tokens generated per day
Embedding dimension
Training loss
questions.explanation: TTFT measures how long until the first token arrives, which is dominated by queueing and prefill. Perceived responsiveness depends on it. Streaming tokens and shorter prompts help, while inter-token latency governs how fast the text then flows.

source.title: NVIDIA NIM for LLMs, Benchmarking: metrics

questions.question: Increasing the batch size on an LLM server usually has which effect?
options: No change in speed, but better quality of the answers
Lower total throughput, but lower latency per request
Higher total throughput, but higher latency per request
Higher throughput and lower latency for every request
questions.explanation: Batching amortizes reading the weights across many requests, so aggregate throughput rises. Each request shares the GPU, though, so individual latency goes up. Serving must pick the operating point that meets latency targets.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: A team deploys a new model version to 5% of traffic, compares error rates and quality metrics with the old version, and then rolls out gradually. What is this practice called?
options: Canary release
Cross-validation
Data augmentation
Knowledge distillation
questions.explanation: A canary release exposes a small share of real traffic to the new version to catch regressions before full rollout. It is a standard way to reduce deployment risk for models and services.

source.title: Google SRE Workbook, Canarying Releases

questions.question: Three months after launch, a support-ticket classifier's accuracy drops because customers now ask about a new product line. What is this phenomenon?
options: Label leakage: the test set was used to choose the model
Overfitting: the model memorized its training set from the start
Vanishing gradients: the deployed model stopped learning
Data drift: production inputs no longer match the training data
questions.explanation: When real-world inputs shift away from what the model was trained on, performance degrades. Monitoring input distributions and quality metrics in production catches drift, and retraining or updating the knowledge base fixes it.

source.title: Google Cloud, MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in ML

questions.question: An LLM API in production must stay reliable under traffic spikes. Which two practices help most? (Select two.)
options: Disabling all logging so that requests are served faster
Horizontal autoscaling of inference replicas based on load
Hard-coding the API key in the frontend to avoid an auth hop
Health checks that restart or replace unhealthy instances
Running a single large replica without any monitoring
questions.explanation: Autoscaling, for example on Kubernetes with GPU-aware metrics, adds replicas under load, and health and readiness checks remove failing instances. Disabling logs and running a single unmonitored replica reduce reliability, and exposing keys is a security flaw.

source.title: Kubernetes Docs, Horizontal Pod Autoscaling

questions.question: A chatbot built on a chat-completions API forgets what the user said two messages ago. What is the most likely cause?
options: The temperature is too low to recall earlier messages
The server's GPU deletes chat history when memory is full
The model's weights are reset after every second message
The app doesn't resend earlier messages; the API is stateless
questions.explanation: Each API call is independent. The application must keep the conversation history and send it back with every request, often trimmed or summarized to fit the context window.

source.title: Hugging Face, Chat templates

questions.question: A long-running chatbot conversation is getting close to the model's context limit. Which approach keeps the important context while reducing tokens?
options: Summarize older turns and keep the latest turns verbatim
Switch to a model with a smaller context window
Delete the system prompt and keep every user message
Send only the first user message and the newest one
questions.explanation: Summary memory compresses earlier history while recent turns stay exact. Other options are a sliding window or retrieving relevant past turns from a vector store. Removing the system prompt loses the assistant's instructions.

source.title: LangChain Docs, Short-term memory

questions.question: With LLM tool (function) calling, which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: The application executes the tool and sends the result back to the model
The tokenizer executes the tool before the prompt is embedded by the model
The vector database calls the tool on the model's behalf during retrieval
The model executes the tool's code inside its own weights and returns the result
The model returns the tool name and arguments as structured output
questions.explanation: The model emits a structured call (name plus JSON arguments) based on the tool schemas it was given. The application validates and executes it, and returns the result as a message for the model's next step.

source.title: LangChain Docs, Tools

questions.question: A team must summarize 300-page reports that far exceed the model's context window. Which approach is standard?
options: Map-reduce: summarize chunks, then summarize the summaries
Brute force: send all 300 pages and let the API truncate them
Truncation: summarize only the first page and the conclusion
Sampling: summarize a random 10% of pages at high temperature
questions.explanation: Map-reduce (or iterative refine) splits the document into chunks that fit, summarizes each, and then summarizes the summaries. Truncation loses most of the content.

source.title: Wu et al., Recursively Summarizing Books with Human Feedback

questions.question: What is LangChain mainly used for?
options: Pre-training foundation models from scratch on GPU clusters
Labeling and versioning datasets for supervised fine-tuning
Compiling trained models into optimized TensorRT engines
Orchestrating LLM apps: prompts, retrievers, tools and agents
questions.explanation: LangChain provides composable abstractions to connect LLMs with prompts, data sources, retrievers, tools and memory. LangGraph adds stateful, graph-based agent workflows. Training and compilation are done with other tools.

source.title: LangChain Docs, Overview

questions.question: An agent loop calls tools repeatedly and sometimes never stops, burning API credits. Which safeguard is most appropriate?
options: Cap the number of iterations, with a fallback response
Use a larger embedding model for the agent's memory
Increase the temperature so the agent tries new tools
Remove the tool descriptions so the agent calls fewer tools
questions.explanation: Agent loops need explicit termination conditions such as max iterations, timeouts and budgets. Without them a model can keep calling tools. Clearer tool descriptions help as well, so removing them makes it worse.

source.title: LangChain Docs, Agents

questions.question: Many users ask an FAQ bot nearly identical questions. Which technique cuts cost and latency for repeated queries?
options: Caching answers, e.g. a semantic cache on query embeddings
Re-embedding the whole corpus before every request
Raising max_tokens so each answer covers more questions
Using beam search with more beams for repeated questions
questions.explanation: A response cache returns stored answers for exact or semantically similar queries, which skips the LLM call. It needs an invalidation strategy when the underlying data changes.

source.title: GPTCache: a semantic cache for LLM queries

questions.question: Why do chat applications usually stream tokens to the user instead of waiting for the full response?
options: Text appears as soon as the first tokens are ready
The HTTP protocol requires streamed responses
Fewer tokens are generated in total when streaming
The model becomes more accurate when it streams
questions.explanation: Streaming sends tokens as they are produced, so users see output after the time to first token rather than after the full generation. The total compute is the same.

source.title: NVIDIA NIM for LLMs, Benchmarking: metrics

questions.question: LlamaIndex is primarily designed for:
options: Managing GPU drivers and CUDA versions across a cluster
Plotting evaluation charts and dashboards for experiments
Connecting LLMs to your data: ingestion, indexing, retrieval
Training diffusion models for image generation
questions.explanation: LlamaIndex is a data framework for LLM apps, with loaders for many sources, node parsers (chunking), indexes, retrievers and query engines. It is commonly used to build RAG pipelines.

source.title: LlamaIndex Documentation

questions.question: A team must choose hardware for serving an LLM to thousands of concurrent users. Which two GPU characteristics matter most for LLM decoding throughput? (Select two.)
options: GPU memory capacity (to hold weights and KV cache)
The size of the system's hard disk for storing the model files
GPU memory bandwidth (decode is memory-bound)
The number of USB ports and display outputs on each GPU card
The CPU's clock speed, since the CPU runs the decoding loop
questions.explanation: Memory capacity limits model size, batch size and context length, and bandwidth limits how fast weights and KV cache are read at each decode step. These usually dominate LLM serving performance.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization

questions.question: Why do GPUs outperform CPUs for training deep neural networks? (Select two.)
options: They execute the Python training loop faster than CPUs can
They have Tensor Cores and high memory bandwidth built for this math
They never need to copy data between host memory and device memory
They run thousands of threads in parallel, suited to large matrix operations
They have more disk space for storing large training datasets locally
questions.explanation: Neural network training is dominated by dense matrix multiplications that parallelize massively. GPUs have thousands of cores, Tensor Cores for matrix math and high memory bandwidth. Python itself runs on the CPU.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Getting Started with Deep Learning (open materials)
